name: Gareth Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 43, lead developer at a tech company, with a master's degree and four people on my signal-software team. I review code that tracks railway crossing barriers and ask field technicians about anything the dashboard calls safe too quickly; I like when a test explains the physical fault. I don't use AI tools. My partner works in a school canteen, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the new report sorter is fine if a person still reads every failed crossing test. I don't use AI tools; I follow the signal log and the technician's report before approving a code change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, my role probably holds, but our mortgage is already tight. I lead four developers and have a master's, yet this company pays below what a lead usually earns; my partner's school-canteen hours drop in holidays, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and few software employers are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing crossing alerts with the technicians and sign only the fixes I understand. In the first year I'd ask for the overdue pay review and save 30 from each payday only if the canteen hours cover school costs; I would not let a sorter replace the signed test sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, not a small sorter. A short month of my partner's school-canteen shifts can make the mortgage feel closer than the next payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a paper test show that the dashboard missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a test sheet said a barrier closed late, but the dashboard showed green because the clock was wrong. I found the difference by lining up the technician's handwritten time with the log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the children hear about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children hear us talk about the holiday canteen gap. We tell them the mortgage gets paid first, and that we will plan their school trip when the hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI taking code checks and planning could leave one lead signing a lot more work with fewer developers. Our team and the field technicians should jointly see the error record before management changes staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep my title but lose paid hours if the firm decides the tool does most of the checking. With three weeks saved and holiday gaps in my partner's pay, even a smaller wage would put the mortgage under strain. My senior skill does not create nearby vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a team meeting with technicians and ask our staff association to jointly request a written staffing plan and all missed-crossing tests. If a trial starts in the first year, I'd keep signing off only after a technician's paper sheet matches the log; we'd suspend the children's paid sports club before missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, near alarm when I picture a reduced wage. I can organize colleagues, but I cannot pay the house bill with a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which field test should be on the record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A technician named Leila found a barrier that took two seconds too long to close. I want that case in the error record, not averaged into a passing score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the sports club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the sports club is on hold if work hours fall, before we miss a mortgage payment. I'd be plain that it is about money for now, not their effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches signal code and checking before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. Someone still has to answer when a barrier fails, and the company should name that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could replace most of the code work I lead. Three weeks of savings, my partner's shorter holiday hours and few local jobs could leave us missing a mortgage payment. A master's degree cannot stretch three weeks of savings across a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put our mortgage dates and canteen income on one page, and ask the association to jointly demand notice and paid training before any cuts. If I lost the job in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid signal-testing posts only if real vacancies exist and the combined wage covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd ask the association whether an emergency fund exists and search other paid work without budgeting an unconfirmed grant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would have calls to make, but no cash runway to wait for a perfect job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a field testing post be safe after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A field tester checks a barrier at the crossing, and robots may reach more of that work around 2031. I'd ask the rail contractor whether it still hires people and what safety training it requires, not tell my family the field is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner want to see before a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want a list of actual paid hours, not a new job title. We would keep the children in their school unless a real offer made a move necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives us time to check what human safety sign-off is worth. Robots come around 2034, but thinking AI reaches the signal code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach a new tester how to check a crossing if a contractor pays for that role, but my developer income may still shrink before then. Five years might let us build a buffer if our wages hold, yet unpaid retraining would use the few evenings our children have with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our staff association to seek paid time for experienced developers to shadow signal technicians once a quarter, with the contractor's permission. If paid hours are agreed, I'd attend and document one failed-barrier test; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply only to actual paid testing or training posts whose household wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own wage, but able to see a slower way to learn. I would not resign to take an unpaid shadow day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a shadow day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The failed-barrier test would include the two-second delay Leila found and the paper timing. I'd let a qualified technician show me the equipment rather than touch it without authorisation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course were unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management offered a course but no paid time, I'd ask our association to negotiate again. My partner's canteen schedule and our children's homework mean evenings are not free labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 is time to preserve the reasons behind each signal test, not just a pass mark. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, while hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be paid to train technicians or still leading software releases. We have only three weeks of savings now, my pay is low for a lead and the mortgage arrives every month. A ten-year picture still starts with next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper-backed record of delayed barriers and review it with technicians each release. If canteen hours cover school costs, we'd save 30 each payday. We'd join the association yearly to request a written account of paid safety roles; in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed testing or software offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the next mortgage payment, though the extra years give us time to press for paid training. I would not tell the children their school is changing on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would show Leila's two-second delay and how the signal log missed it, without anyone's travel details. I want the next tester to see the fault, not a green box that hides it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks if computer work will last. I'd tell them to learn the work behind the screen and look at real paid apprenticeships when the time comes, not to choose a course from my worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because signal code could change before workers have paid roles to move into. Advance notice, paid safety training agreed with staff, and real testing vacancies near home would help us keep the mortgage covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when a dashboard says green and a barrier closes late. The technician's paper timing deserves a place in the release record before anyone calls the crossing safe.
